passage:
Parenting notebook, 3 March.
Nitin (5) knocked the clay pot off the balcony ledge while racing his car. I heard the crash. "Who did this?" nearly came out. I stopped, because that question would only get me "Not me."
Instead I said, "The pot fell. Are you okay?" He nodded, eyes huge. Then he whispered, "My car hit it."
I told him, "Thank you for telling me. The truth matters more to me than any pot." We swept up together. He kept checking my face, but by bedtime he was choosing a plant for a new pot.
Ayesha

qa.q: What did Nitin knock off the balcony ledge?
qa.a: He knocked the clay pot off the balcony ledge while racing his car.

qa.q: What does Nitin checking Ayesha's face suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was still a little worried about being in trouble, even after being thanked.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha avoid asking "Who did this?"
qa.a: That question would only invite "Not me", so Ayesha described what happened and checked he was okay, making the truth easy to say.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Nitin whispered, "My car hit it"?
qa.a: Ayesha likely felt glad and grateful that Nitin told the truth, which is why Ayesha thanked him and said the truth mattered more than any pot.

grounding: A parent avoids the 'who did this' trap, says the truth matters more than the pot, and meets a small boy's confession with calm repair and thanks.

passage:
At dusk the village hens were scattered all over the lane. Chaitanya saw the coop door swinging open. His daughter Deepika, five, stood by the neem tree with her hands behind her back.
He did not ask, "Who opened it?" He crouched and said, "The hens are out. The truth matters more to me than hens. What happened?"
Deepika's lip shook. "I wanted to hold the brown one. I forgot to close it."
"Thank you for telling me," he said. "Now let's catch them before dark." They chased the hens together, Deepika laughing.

qa.q: Where was Deepika standing when Chaitanya saw the open coop?
qa.a: She stood by the neem tree with her hands behind her back.

qa.q: What does Deepika's shaking lip show?
qa.a: It shows she was scared of being scolded for letting the hens out.

qa.q: What made it easy for Deepika to confess?
qa.a: Chaitanya avoided asking who opened it, said the truth mattered more than hens, thanked her, and then fixed the problem with her.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel about her father after the evening?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and close to him, laughing as they chased the hens, and safer telling the truth next time.

grounding: A father in a village avoids a blaming question, tells his daughter the truth matters more than the mistake, and repairs it with her calmly.

passage:
Chidi came out of the kitchen of their London flat and saw blue crayon all over the hallway wall. Mei stood very still, holding a blue crayon.
He didn't ask, "Who did this?" That would only invite a "Not me."
He knelt down. "I see drawing on the wall. Let's get a cloth."
Mei's lip trembled. "I did it, Daddy. I wanted a big picture."
"Thank you for telling me. That matters more than the wall."
They scrubbed together. Then he taped a big sheet of paper up. "Big pictures go here." Mei beamed.

qa.q: What colour was the crayon on the wall?
qa.a: It was blue crayon.

qa.q: Why did Chidi avoid asking "Who did this?"
qa.a: Chidi felt calm and wanted to make the truth easy, knowing that question would only invite a "Not me."

qa.q: What did Chidi do that made truth feel safe?
qa.a: He named what he saw, thanked Mei for confessing, said telling mattered more than the wall, and repaired it together with her.

qa.q: How does Mei feel when her father thanks her?
qa.a: Mei feels relieved and happy, beaming at the big sheet of paper he taped up.

grounding: It shows a father avoiding a trap question, thanking his daughter for confessing and calmly repairing the wall together.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, a page of Tenzin's picture magazine tore right across. He looked up quickly at his mother.
Indu didn't ask, "Did you do that?" She sat beside him. "Oh, the page tore."
Tenzin stared at his shoes. "I pulled it too hard."
"Thank you for telling me. That was honest. Shall we tell the lady at the desk together?"
At the counter, Tenzin held it up. "I tore it. Sorry."
The receptionist smiled. "Thank you for telling me. We have tape."
Tenzin walked back to his chair, standing a little taller.

qa.q: Where were Tenzin and his mother?
qa.a: In the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when he looked up at his mother after the page tore?
qa.a: Tenzin felt worried and nervous that he would be in trouble for tearing it.

qa.q: What did Indu do instead of asking "Did you do that?"
qa.a: She named what happened calmly, thanked him for telling the truth, and went with him to tell the receptionist.

qa.q: How does the receptionist react to Tenzin's confession?
qa.a: The receptionist smiles kindly, thanks him and offers tape, which makes telling the truth feel good.

grounding: It shows a mother avoiding a trap question, thanking her son for confessing and calmly repairing the mistake with him.

passage:
I live across the courtyard from Jagdish and his son Deepak. On Sunday, through my kitchen window, I heard a crash. A clay pot lay in pieces by Deepak's ball. Deepak froze.
Jagdish came out. He didn't shout, "Who broke it?" He crouched. "Pot broke. Want to help me clean it?"
Deepak's chin wobbled. "I kicked the ball there."
"Thank you for telling me. That's more important than a pot."
They swept up the pieces together. I couldn't hear the rest, but Deepak ran back to his ball, smiling.

qa.q: What lay in pieces by Deepak's ball?
qa.a: A clay pot lay in pieces.

qa.q: How did Deepak seem to feel right after the crash?
qa.a: Deepak seemed frightened and unsure, freezing after the crash, then relieved after he confessed.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do instead of shouting?
qa.a: He crouched, named the broken pot, invited Deepak to help clean it, and thanked him for telling the truth.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Jagdish's response?
qa.a: The neighbour finds it memorable and warm, though they could not hear everything, noticing Deepak ran back smiling.

grounding: A neighbour observes a father avoiding a trap question, thanking his young son for confessing, and calmly repairing the broken pot together.

passage:
Monday: Binita found blue paint on the new rug. "Who did this?" she asked sharply. Gurleen, five, said, "Not me. The cat." They didn't have a cat.
Wednesday: Binita tried something else. She saw juice on the sofa and said calmly, "I see juice on the sofa. Let's clean it together." Gurleen fetched the cloth. "I spilled it," she whispered. Binita said, "Thank you for telling me. Being honest is more important to me than any spill."
The next Tuesday: Gurleen came running into the kitchen. "Mumma, I broke the crayon box. I'm telling the truth!" Binita knelt, hugged her, and they taped the box up together.

qa.q: Who did Gurleen blame for the paint?
qa.a: The cat, though they didn't have a cat.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when Gurleen came running about the crayon box?
qa.a: Binita felt touched and proud, kneeling to hug Gurleen after seeing the change.

qa.q: What changed in Binita's approach, and why did it work?
qa.a: She stopped asking 'Who did this?', named what she saw calmly, cleaned up together and thanked Gurleen for the truth, so honesty felt safe.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have blamed the cat on Monday?
qa.a: Gurleen was scared by the sharp question and grabbed the first escape, since 'Who did this?' made the truth feel dangerous.

grounding: Shows a parent dropping 'who did this' and meeting confessions with calm repair and thanks, so the child learns the truth is safe.
